title: The Flying Scroll and the Woman in the Basket
summary: In the sixth vision Zechariah sees an enormous flying scroll, a curse going out over the land against thieves and those who swear falsely by God's name, which enters their houses and destroys them. In the seventh he sees a measuring basket with a woman inside, named Wickedness, pushed down under a lead cover and carried away by two winged women to a house built for it in the land of Shinar.
story: The earlier visions promised that God would return to Jerusalem, cleanse the high priest, and complete the temple by his Spirit. But a rebuilt temple in the middle of a corrupt community would contradict itself. These two visions deal with the sin of the people as a whole. The first announces that God's law will judge wrongdoing within the community; the second shows wickedness itself removed from the land and sent back to Babylon, where exile began. After this, only the eighth vision (6:1-8) remains, returning to the horses and chariots of the first. Together the fourth to seventh visions make a single point: God is making both his leaders and his land clean enough for him to live among them.
historical:
The community around Jerusalem in 519 BC faced ordinary but corrosive sins. Haggai had described economic hardship (Haggai 1:6-11), and in such times theft and false oaths in business and at law flourish. A generation later Nehemiah would confront wealthy Judeans for exploiting poorer neighbors (Nehemiah 5), and Malachi would condemn those who swear falsely and defraud workers (Malachi 3:5). The two crimes named on the scroll, theft and swearing falsely by God's name, correspond to the eighth and third commandments (Exodus 20:7, 15), and many interpreters take them as representing the two tablets of the law, sins against neighbor and against God.

Shinar is an old name for the land of Babylonia, the plain where the tower of Babel was built (Genesis 11:2). Sending wickedness there reverses the exile: the people had been carried to Babylon for their sin; now the sin is carried to Babylon and the people remain.
cultural:
The scroll is huge: twenty cubits by ten, about thirty feet by fifteen (roughly 9 by 4.5 meters), if a cubit is taken as about eighteen inches. Those are the dimensions of the porch of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:3), which may suggest that the curse goes out from God's presence. Scrolls were normally written on one side only; this one, like the tablets of the law (Exodus 32:15), has writing on both sides. In the ancient world a curse was a solemn declaration invoking divine punishment on anyone who broke an oath or covenant, and the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 27 and 28 hang behind this vision.

The ephah was a standard dry measure for grain, probably a little over twenty liters, and the basket in the vision is a container sized to hold that amount; the BSB calls it a measuring basket. The round lead cover is literally a talent of lead, a talent being a large standard weight. The two women have wings like a stork. The stork was an unclean bird in the law (Leviticus 11:19), but it was known for long migrations, which may be the point: they carry the basket far away. Its Hebrew name, chasidah, sounds like the word for loyal love (chesed), and some scholars see a play on words. The pedestal in verse 11 may suggest a base on which an image stands in a shrine, as though wickedness will be worshiped in its proper home.
literary: These are the sixth and seventh visions, each following the pattern of seeing, asking, and explanation. The first is quick and forceful: a scroll that flies, enters houses, and consumes them down to the wood and stones. The second is more elaborate and almost comic in its details: a heavy lid lifted, a woman who tries to get out, the angel shoving her back and slamming down the lead. Both visions personify evil (a curse that travels, a woman who is Wickedness) and use motion to show God removing sin. The Hebrew word for wickedness is feminine, which likely explains why it is pictured as a woman.

outline.t: Sixth vision: the flying scroll, a curse on thieves and perjurers
Seventh vision: Wickedness in the measuring basket
The basket carried to a house in Shinar

doctrines.note: The curse written on both sides of the scroll names theft and perjury, sins against neighbor and against God's name. God's law is not a dead letter; it goes out into every house, and the covenant's warnings remain in force for the restored community.
Wickedness is pictured as a living power that tries to escape, not merely a list of wrong acts. God does not ignore it or leave it in the land; he confines it and carries it away.
A holy God cannot dwell among a people who harbor wickedness. The removal of sin from the land prepares a clean place for God's presence, the goal of all the visions.

words.note: Alah, an oath or curse. It means a solemn statement invoking punishment on oneself or others if a commitment is broken, and it is used of covenant curses (Deuteronomy 29:12, 14). The scroll carries the curse attached to God's covenant, now let loose against those who break it.

Rishah, wickedness or guilt. It describes moral evil as the opposite of righteousness. In verse 8 it becomes a name, This is Wickedness, and the vision shows it being removed from the land by God's agents.

Ayin, usually eye, but here in verse 6 the traditional Hebrew text reads their eye (or appearance) in all the land. Ancient Greek and Syriac translations read their iniquity, a very similar word in Hebrew, and the BSB and many translations follow them. The text is uncertain, but either reading says the basket holds what the people are like.

Shinar, the old name for Babylonia. It is the land where Babel's builders tried to make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:2-4). Returning wickedness to Shinar sends it back to the Bible's symbolic home of human pride and rebellion.

christ: This chapter's link to Christ is thematic, not predictive. Its picture of sin carried away from the land recalls the scapegoat of the Day of Atonement, which bore the people's sins into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21-22), and the New Testament sees that removal accomplished in Christ, who bore our sins in his body (1 Peter 2:24). Paul says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so the curse that the flying scroll carries into the houses of the guilty is, in the gospel, borne by Christ himself. Revelation's picture of Babylon the great as a woman in whom the world's wickedness is gathered and finally judged (Revelation 17 and 18) draws on the same symbolic world as Zechariah's woman sent to Shinar.

hard.q: Why is wickedness pictured as a woman, and does the passage demean women?
hard.a: The most straightforward answer is grammatical. The Hebrew word for wickedness, rishah, is feminine, as are many abstract nouns in Hebrew, and prophetic visions often personify such nouns as women; Proverbs does the same with Wisdom (Proverbs 8) and Folly (Proverbs 9:13). In the same vision, the agents God uses to carry wickedness away are also women, with wings, so the passage is not setting women as such against God. Some scholars also suggest a specific background: the pedestal in Shinar may point to idol worship, and the woman may recall a goddess figure such as the Queen of Heaven condemned by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 44:17-19), so that the vision pictures idolatry being carried out of the land. Readers should take the woman as a symbol of evil, not a statement about women.

questions: Theft and false oaths are ordinary sins. Why does God treat them as seriously as he does, even in a community focused on rebuilding his temple?
The woman in the basket tries to rise and has to be pushed back down. How have you experienced the persistence of sin in your own life?
God does not merely forgive the land; he removes wickedness from it. What would it mean for you to let him carry something out of your life entirely?
